name: Wei Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick and pack at an electronics distribution warehouse: phone cases, chargers, headphones, small stuff in small boxes, thousands of orders a day. I'm on the late shift, two till half ten. Half my day is picking, and the other half, unofficially, is getting the floor robots unstuck when they freeze at a junction. Nobody gave me that job, I just figured out how they work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up being the one who fixes the robots?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Curiosity, mostly. Two years ago one stopped in front of me and the engineer was on break, so I asked a chatbot on my phone what the error code meant and reset it. Now the shift lead shouts for me before the engineer. I don't get paid extra for it, which is a sore point, but I like it more than the picking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly, because I use AI every day and I like it. At work I'd say the robots we have are still the future of this place. Online I'd probably argue that the hype hurt people, because bosses used it as an excuse to squeeze wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it changes very little. I've got about a year's pay saved and some money in an index fund, and my boyfriend Sam teaches at a primary school. The robots on our floor keep getting better on their own, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push my manager to make the robot-fixing official, with a title and a pay bump. If they said no, I'd apply at the parcel hub across the road, which is hiring technicians. And I'd start an evening course in electrical basics this spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. I'd still be excited about the robots, just less about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You fix robots for free. How long would you put up with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six months, tops. I've already told Ana, my shift lead, what I'm doing. I keep a log of every robot reset I do for free. Last month it was forty-one, and that's a number I can put in front of HR.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the union help with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I'd bring the rep in if HR stalls. It's not just me, there's a woman on days, Grace, who does the same on the conveyor. If we both get recognised, it sets a rule for everyone who picks up extra skills.

say: He's a bit **disappointed**, because he uses AI daily and likes it.
Bosses used the **hype** as an excuse to squeeze wages, he'd argue online.
think: With **a year saved** and an index fund, little changes for him personally.
The **floor robots** keep improving anyway, AI or no AI.
do: Push his manager to make **robot fixing** an official, paid role.
Apply at the **parcel hub** across the road if refused.
Start an **evening electrical course** this spring.
feel: **Calm** and a bit flat, still excited about robots but less about AI.
S0.quote: I keep a log of every robot reset I do for free. Last month it was forty-one, and that's a number I can put in front of HR.
fieldNote: He has quietly become the floor's **robot fixer** without pay or title.
Uses AI daily and treats robots as **opportunity**, not threat.
Brings the **union** in to make extra skills count for everyone, not just him.

steps.text: Show HR his log of forty-one robot resets and ask for a technician title
Start an evening electrical basics course this spring
Bring the union rep in if HR stalls on recognition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get skilled up, and I'd say it loudly in the canteen. I'd share free course links in our work group chat. And I'd say the company should pay for it, because they'll save a fortune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's good for me. More robots spreading slowly means more robots breaking, and I'm the guy who fixes them. The ones I'd worry about are the office people, like the stock controllers who check numbers all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the electrical course and apply for an official robot technician job inside a year, here or across the road. I'd use AI tools even more to read manuals and fault logs. And I'd keep saving, because a new job might mean a short probation with less overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. It's the first time the change is going my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the pickers who aren't into tech?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth. Most robot freezes are a dirty sensor or a box in the wrong place. The error codes aren't magic. I'd run a lunchtime session if the company let me, because I don't want to be the only one who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's good for you. Does anything about it bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stock control team. There's a guy, Tunde, who's been counting stock for fifteen years and doesn't use a computer outside work. If AI does his checks, he's fifty-one with nothing lined up. That bothers me more than my own job.

say: This is the moment to get **skilled up**, and the company should **pay** for it.
He'd share **free course links** in the work group chat.
think: More robots means more **breakdowns**, which is good for the guy who fixes them.
The **stock controllers** who check numbers all day are most at risk.
do: Finish the **electrical course** and apply for a **technician job** within a year.
Use AI tools more to read **manuals and fault logs**.
Keep saving in case a new job means **lower overtime** at first.
feel: **Calm**, even a bit **excited**, since change is finally going his way.
S1.quote: Most robot freezes are a dirty sensor or a box in the wrong place. The error codes aren't magic.
fieldNote: Steady Disruption looks like **promotion** to him; robots that break need fixers.
Wants to **teach others** rather than hoard the skill.
Worries for **older colleagues** like Tunde (a stock controller, fifty-one) more than himself.

steps.text: Apply for an official robot technician job within a year
Read robot manuals and fault logs with AI tools
Run lunchtime sessions teaching pickers basic robot resets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, fast, because two years isn't enough for governments to do anything else. I'd join the union push for proper redundancy and I'd go on a march. Online I'd be the guy posting long threads about who owns the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my robot-fixing gives me a head start, but it's a short one. The thinking AI in 2028 could diagnose faults better than me, so I'd become the hands that swap the part. Then by 2031 the robots swap their own parts. I'd have maybe five good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get my technician job and work every bit of overtime while it pays well. I'd save hard, maybe 60 percent of my pay, because I'd want two or three years of cushion by 2031. I'd also put some of the index fund money into the companies making the robots, since that's where the money goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, I've got money and skills. Even the guy who fixes the robots gets replaced when the robots learn to swap their own parts. That's a weird thing to sit with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're left-leaning and you'd buy robot company shares. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, a bit. But if the robots are coming anyway, I'd rather own a tiny piece than none. Sam calls it my hypocrite fund. I'd still vote for taxing them hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sam talk about at dinner that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether teaching is safe. Sam thinks kids will always need a real teacher in the room, and I'd probably agree. So we'd talk about Sam's income being the steady one and mine being the risky one for a while.

say: Two years is too short for anything but a **basic income**, and fast.
He'd post long threads online about **who owns the robots**.
think: Thinking AI in 2028 would **diagnose faults** better than him, leaving him the hands.
By 2031 robots swap their own parts, giving him maybe **five good years**.
do: Take the **technician job** and all the overtime he can in the first year.
Save about **60 percent** of his pay for two or three years of cushion.
Move part of his index fund into **robot makers**.
feel: **Anxious**, though not panicked, because of his **money and skills**.
Finds it **strange** that even the robot fixer gets replaced.
S2.quote: Even the guy who fixes the robots gets replaced when the robots learn to swap their own parts.
fieldNote: He maps the **3-year gap** precisely: thinking AI takes diagnosis first, then robots take his hands.
Owns his contradiction: buys **robot shares** while voting to tax robots.
His partner's teaching job is the **household anchor**.

steps.text: Take the technician job and work maximum overtime this year
Save about 60 percent of pay until 2031
Move part of the index fund into robot makers' shares
March with the union for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if we start today, and I'd be pushing the union to win a training fund now. I'd tell friends to learn the machines, not fight them. I'd keep posting about robot taxes, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years to AGI and eight to the robots means I'd be thirty-five when the hands-on side goes. That's long enough to become properly good, maybe a controls engineer rather than just a reset guy. The higher I climb, the later I get replaced. A controls engineer lasts longer than a reset guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the technician job and then a two-year part-time course in automation and control systems. I'd use AI tools to study every evening. I'd save less hard than in the two-year one, maybe 30 percent, and keep the rest in the index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not worse. It's a challenge I'd almost enjoy if I didn't know where it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does it end, in your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2034, robots that fix robots. So the climb buys me time but not forever. By then I'd want something people pay a human for, maybe teaching technicians, or running a small repair business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything about how I'd sleep. With two years I'm grabbing money. With five I'm building skills, and skills feel better than a pile of cash. Sam says I'd be unbearable about it, and that's fair.

say: **Five years** is enough if everyone starts today, including a union **training fund**.
He'd tell friends to **learn the machines**, not fight them.
think: He'd be **thirty-five** when the hands-on side goes, long enough to climb.
The higher he climbs, from reset guy to **controls engineer**, the later he's replaced.
do: Take the **technician job**, then a two-year **automation course** part-time.
Save about **30 percent**, keeping the rest in the index fund.
feel: **Uneasy**, almost enjoying the challenge, if not for knowing where it ends.
S3.quote: The higher I climb, the later I get replaced. A controls engineer lasts longer than a reset guy.
fieldNote: More warning moves him from **grabbing money** to **building skills**.
Sees his ladder clearly: reset guy, technician, **controls engineer**.
Admits the climb has an **end point** around 2034.

steps.text: Enrol in a two-year part-time automation and control course
Study course material every evening with AI tools
Save about 30 percent of pay and keep the index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the best version of this, and if we waste it, that's on politicians, not on technology. I'd push for robot taxes funding retraining and a shorter week. At work I'd say learn now while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is plenty for me. I'd be thirty-seven at AGI and forty when the robots match people. By then I could have my own small automation repair business, or be training others, and I'd have savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take the technician job and start the automation course. In five years I'd want to start a small firm fixing robots for smaller warehouses that can't afford their own engineers. I'd use AI for the business side from day one, quotes, invoices, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Genuinely. The ten-year picture is the first one where I feel like my plan is bigger than the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A business is a big step. What would you put into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe 20 thousand of savings, a van and some test kit. I wouldn't quit the day job until I had three steady clients. Sam would insist on that, and Sam would be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at work would you bring with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace from the conveyor, if she wanted. She knows belts and motors better than me. I'd want it to be a proper co-op, where the people doing the work own a share.

say: Ten years is the **best version**; wasting it would be on **politicians**.
He'd urge colleagues to **learn now** while there's time.
think: At **forty** when robots match people, he could run his **own repair firm**.
Ten years is **plenty** for someone with savings and skills.
do: Take the **technician job** and start the automation course in year one.
Plan a small **robot repair firm** for smaller warehouses within five years.
Use AI for **quotes and invoices** from day one.
feel: **Calm**, feeling the plan is **bigger** than the problem.
S4.quote: The ten-year picture is the first one where I feel like my plan is bigger than the problem.
fieldNote: With a decade he'd build a **co-op repair firm**, mixing his politics with his skills.
Careful with money: no quitting until **three steady clients**.
Sees colleague Grace (a conveyor fixer) as a **future partner**.

steps.text: Take the technician job and start the automation course

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even my best skill gets swallowed and there's no time to climb. What would help is a training fund that pays a wage while you learn, and companies having to tell workers years ahead what they're automating.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about being paid for skills you picked up yourself. Half the people keeping warehouses running are doing jobs nobody hired them for. If companies paid for that now, people would trust the change more.

headlineQuote: Half the people keeping warehouses running are doing jobs nobody hired them for.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old picker** at an electronics warehouse who has become the floor's unpaid **robot fixer**.
He uses AI daily, has **a year's pay saved**, and lives with Sam, a primary school teacher.
He's progressive and pro-union, yet sees robots as his **ladder up**.
The **2-year AGI** picture makes him anxious; with ten years he'd start a co-op **repair firm**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even his robot-fixing skill gets swallowed with no time to climb.
whatWouldHelp: A **training fund** paying a wage while people learn.
Companies telling workers **years ahead** what they'll automate.
